early_history_summary: Born to NBC president Pat Weaver and English actress Elizabeth Inglis, Weaver attended Stanford and Yale Drama School, graduating in 1974. She performed in off-Broadway shows and made a brief Broadway debut in 1974, but had no major film or stage milestone by age 26.
family_context_summary: Daughter of NBC president Sylvester 'Pat' Weaver and English actress Elizabeth Inglis; grew up in New York City's media elite.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a television executive (NBC president); mother was a professional actress — strong entertainment industry lineage.

name: Ilan Pappé
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: completed BA at Hebrew University in 1978 (age 24) but DPhil from Oxford came in 1984 (age 30); first book derived from doctoral thesis published after 26. No material academic milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Haifa to German Jewish parents who fled Nazi persecution, Pappé was drafted into the IDF at 18 and served in the Yom Kippur War. He completed his BA at Hebrew University in 1978 before moving to Oxford for his doctorate, which he completed in 1984.
family_context_summary: Born to Ashkenazi Jewish parents in Haifa who were German Jews that fled Nazi persecution in the 1930s.
evidence_summary: Pappé completed his BA at Hebrew University by 1978 and began doctoral studies at Oxford, but his DPhil and first book did not arrive until 1984 when he was 30. No material milestone by age 26 was identified.

name: Mike Bossy
milestone_by_age_26: In his 1977-78 NHL rookie season at age 20-21, Bossy scored 53 goals (an NHL rookie record) and won the Calder Memorial Trophy as rookie of the year; he went on to win four consecutive Stanley Cups by age 26.
early_history_summary: The fifth of ten children in a working-class Montreal family, Bossy learned to skate at age three on a backyard rink his father built. He starred in the QMJHL for the Laval Nationals, scoring 309 goals in five junior seasons, before being drafted 15th overall by the New York Islanders in 1977 and immediately becoming the first rookie to score 50 goals in NHL history.
family_context_summary: Fifth of ten children in a working-class Montreal family; father Borden (Ukrainian) maintained a backyard ice rink, mother Dorothy was English and French-Canadian. Family was not poor but could not afford anything special with ten children.
parent_family_domain_summary: Hockey-saturated family: father planted a hockey stick in Mike's crib, maintained a backyard rink, and mother sent birthday cards to Gordie Howe. Two brothers also played hockey with Mike.
primary_early_advantage_tags: backyard rink, hockey family, Montreal, junior hockey pipeline, early scoring talent
evidence_summary: Bossy grew up in a hockey-obsessed working-class Montreal family with a backyard rink built by his father. He started skating at three, dominated youth hockey, and scored 309 goals in five QMJHL seasons before his NHL rookie year. At age 20-21, he set the NHL rookie goal record (53) and won the Calder Trophy, launching a career that included four straight Stanley Cups by age 26. His early advantage came from deep domain immersion in Montreal's hockey culture and extensive early reps rather than financial resources.
starting_point: Born in 1957 in working-class Montreal, the fifth of ten children; father was a craftsman of Ukrainian descent who built a backyard rink, mother was English and French-Canadian.
current_position: Died April 15, 2022 at age 65 in Rosemère, Quebec; final role: NHL broadcaster and hockey stick company executive after retirement from playing.

trajectory.event: Scored 53 goals as an NHL rookie with the New York Islanders, winning the Calder Memorial Trophy and setting the all-time rookie goal record.
Won his first of four consecutive Stanley Cup championships with the New York Islanders.
Won the Conn Smythe Trophy as playoff MVP and scored the Stanley Cup-winning goal for the second straight year.
Won his fourth consecutive Stanley Cup, scoring the Cup-winning goal for the third consecutive year.
Retired from the NHL due to chronic back problems, finishing with 573 goals in 752 games over 10 seasons.
Inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame in his first year of eligibility.
Died on April 15, 2022, in Rosemère, Quebec, after a battle with lung cancer.

name: Erich von Däniken
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: first published article appeared in 1964 (age 29) and first book 'Chariots of the Gods?' was published in 1968 (age 33); no material writing milestone by age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Zofingen, Switzerland, von Däniken attended a Catholic school and developed an early interest in biblical inconsistencies and ancient astronauts. He worked in hotels after leaving school, traveled widely, and was convicted of fraud and embezzlement in Egypt before writing his bestselling first book in 1968.
family_context_summary: Brought up in a conservative Roman Catholic setting in Switzerland; attended Saint-Michel International Catholic School in Fribourg.
evidence_summary: Von Däniken worked in hotels and traveled extensively as a young man, but his first published article did not appear until 1964 (age 29) and his landmark book 'Chariots of the Gods?' was published in 1968 (age 33). No material writing milestone by age 26 was found.

early_history_summary: Born in Brede, Denmark, August studied photography in Stockholm and then at the National Film School of Denmark, graduating in 1973. He worked as a cinematographer before making his feature directorial debut in 1978 with 'In My Life,' which won the Bodil Award for Best Danish Film.
family_context_summary: Born in Brede, Denmark; attended photography school in Stockholm before entering the National Film School of Denmark.

name: Mario Lemieux
milestone_by_age_26: In his 1984-85 NHL rookie season at age 19, Lemieux scored 100 points, won the Calder Memorial Trophy as rookie of the year, and became the first rookie named All-Star Game MVP; he later won two Stanley Cups and multiple MVP awards by age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in working-class Ville-Émard, Montreal, Lemieux started skating at age three, using kitchen spoons as sticks and bottle caps as pucks. His father built a front-lawn rink and the family packed snow on the hallway carpet for indoor practice. He dominated Quebec junior hockey, setting a QMJHL record of 282 points in 70 games in 1983-84, before being drafted first overall by the Pittsburgh Penguins in 1984.
family_context_summary: Born to a working-class family in Ville-Émard, Montreal; father Jean-Guy worked in construction/engineering, mother Pierrette was a stay-at-home mom. Youngest of three hockey-playing brothers in a four-room apartment.
parent_family_domain_summary: Hockey-immersed family: father built a front-lawn rink, mother packed snow on the hallway carpet for indoor skating, and all three brothers played hockey obsessively from early childhood.
primary_early_advantage_tags: backyard rink, hockey family, Montreal, QMJHL dominance, early talent, dropped out of school
evidence_summary: Lemieux grew up in a working-class Montreal household saturated with hockey — his father built a rink on the front lawn and his mother packed snow on the hallway carpet for indoor practice. He started skating at three, dropped out of school at 16 to focus on hockey, and set a QMJHL record of 282 points in 70 games at age 18. Drafted first overall in 1984, he scored 100 points as a rookie at 19, winning the Calder Trophy and All-Star Game MVP. His advantages were extreme early domain immersion, a prodigy-level physical talent, and Montreal's hockey ecosystem rather than financial resources.
starting_point: Born in 1965 in working-class Ville-Émard, Montreal; father worked in construction, mother was a homemaker, youngest of three brothers in a four-room apartment.
current_position: Part-owner and chairman of the Pittsburgh Penguins; estimated net worth ~$200M; resides in Sewickley, Pennsylvania.

trajectory.event: Drafted first overall by the Pittsburgh Penguins and scored 100 points in his rookie NHL season, winning the Calder Trophy and becoming the first rookie named All-Star Game MVP.
Won his first Hart Trophy as NHL MVP and first Art Ross Trophy as scoring champion with 168 points.
Won his first Stanley Cup with the Pittsburgh Penguins after returning from back surgery mid-season.
Won his second consecutive Stanley Cup with the Penguins, scoring 16 goals in 15 playoff games.
Diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma during the season but returned to win his third scoring title despite missing two months of play.
Retired from hockey for the first time due to chronic health problems, having scored 613 goals in 745 games.
Purchased the then-bankrupt Pittsburgh Penguins, becoming the first former player to own his former team in major professional sports.
Returned to play in the NHL as player-owner, becoming the first owner-player in modern professional sports.

name: Jason Day
milestone_by_age_26: At age 19 in July 2007, Day became the youngest winner in Nationwide Tour (now Korn Ferry Tour) history at the Legend Financial Group Classic; he earned his PGA Tour card that year and won his first PGA Tour event at age 22 in 2010.
early_history_summary: Born in Beaudesert, Queensland, Day was introduced to golf at age six by his father, who enrolled him as a junior member at the local golf club. After his father died of stomach cancer when Jason was 12, his mother sold the family home to send him to a golf boarding school, where coach Col Swatton became his mentor and father figure. Inspired by a Tiger Woods book, he practiced intensively and won the Callaway Junior World Championship at 16 before turning pro at 18.
family_context_summary: Father Alvin was Irish Australian who worked at a meatworks and died of stomach cancer when Jason was 12; mother Dening was a Filipino immigrant who sold the family home to fund Jason's golf education. Two siblings.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father introduced Jason to golf at age six and enrolled him as a junior member at Beaudesert Golf Club, giving him a rusty three-iron found at a junkyard. No prior family golf expertise beyond this introduction.
primary_early_advantage_tags: golf academy, Col Swatton mentor, father's death, mother's sacrifice, Tiger Woods inspiration, junior golf
evidence_summary: Day's early path was shaped by adversity — his father died when he was 12, leaving the family in poverty — and by the intervention of coach Col Swatton, who became his sustained mentor and father figure at a golf boarding school. His mother sold the family home to fund his golf education. Day practiced up to 30 hours per week, won the Junior World Championship at 16, turned pro at 18, and became the youngest Nationwide Tour winner at 19. His advantages were a dedicated mentor, access to a golf academy, and intense self-driven practice rather than financial resources or family golf lineage.
starting_point: Born in 1987 in Beaudesert, Queensland, Australia; father was an Irish Australian meatworker who died when Jason was 12, mother was a Filipino immigrant who sold the family home to fund his golf training.
current_position: Active PGA Tour golfer with 13 PGA Tour wins including the 2015 PGA Championship; former World No. 1 (2015-2017); resides in Westerville, Ohio.

trajectory.event: Became the youngest winner in Nationwide Tour history at the Legend Financial Group Classic, earning his PGA Tour card for the following season.
Won his first PGA Tour event at the HP Byron Nelson Championship, becoming the youngest Australian to win a PGA Tour event.
Finished runner-up at the Masters and the U.S. Open, establishing himself among golf's elite.
Won the PGA Championship for his first major title and reached World No. 1 in the Official World Golf Ranking.
Won THE PLAYERS Championship and held the World No. 1 ranking for 51 weeks total.
Won the AT&T Byron Nelson, his first PGA Tour victory in five years, returning to the winner's circle.

name: Robin Gibb
milestone_by_age_26: At age 17 in 1967, Robin Gibb co-wrote and sang lead on 'New York Mining Disaster 1941,' the Bee Gees' first international hit, followed by 'Massachusetts' which reached UK No. 1 that same year; the group had already scored an Australian No. 1 with 'Spicks and Specks' in 1966.
early_history_summary: Born on the Isle of Man to a musical family — father Hugh was a drummer and bandleader, mother Barbara was a dance-band vocalist — Robin began performing with brothers Barry and Maurice from age six. The family emigrated to Brisbane, Australia in 1958, where the brothers performed at racetracks and on TV, signed to Festival Records in 1963, and scored their first Australian No. 1 in 1966 before returning to England and achieving worldwide fame in 1967.
family_context_summary: Born to Hugh Gibb (drummer, bandleader, chauffeur) and Barbara Gibb (née Pass, former dance-band vocalist) on the Isle of Man. Family was poor — father counted coins for meals of chip butties — and emigrated from Manchester to Brisbane, Australia in 1958 seeking work.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were musical professionals: father Hugh was a drummer and bandleader who formed the Hughie Gibb Orchestra, mother Barbara was a dance-band vocalist. Father managed and promoted the brothers' early career.
primary_early_advantage_tags: musical parents, brother trio, early performing, Australian TV, Festival Records, British Invasion, poverty
evidence_summary: Robin Gibb's early advantage was deeply rooted in a musical family — both parents were professional musicians who nurtured the brothers' performing careers from age six. The tight sibling trio (Robin, Barry, and twin Maurice) performed constantly at cinemas, racetracks, and on Australian TV throughout their early teens, accumulating thousands of hours of stage experience before their first international hit at 17. The family's poverty and emigration to Australia created urgency and opportunity. Their father managed and promoted them, and the 1960s pop music wave provided the structural tailwind for their breakthrough.
starting_point: Born in 1949 on the Isle of Man to a poor musical family; father was a drummer/bandleader who worked menial day jobs, mother was a former dance-band vocalist; family emigrated to Brisbane, Australia in 1958.
current_position: Died May 20, 2012 at age 62 in London, England; final role: Bee Gees member and solo artist, CBE honoree.

trajectory.event: The Bee Gees signed their first recording contract with Leedon Records in Australia and released their debut single.
The Bee Gees scored their first Australian No. 1 hit with 'Spicks and Specks,' establishing them as local stars.
Returned to England, signed with manager Robert Stigwood, and released 'New York Mining Disaster 1941' — their first international hit — followed by 'Massachusetts' which reached UK No. 1.
Left the Bee Gees for a solo career, scoring a UK No. 2 hit with 'Saved by the Bell' before reuniting with the group.
The Bee Gees released the Saturday Night Fever soundtrack, which became the best-selling album in history at that time and cemented their global superstardom.
The Bee Gees were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
Appointed CBE (Commander of the Order of the British Empire) along with brothers Barry and Maurice for contributions to music.
Died on May 20, 2012, in London after a long battle with cancer.

name: Ferdinand Alexander Porsche
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: joined Porsche in 1958 (age 22-23) and took over the design studio around 1962 (age 26-27), but the Porsche 911 — his landmark design — was unveiled at the Frankfurt Motor Show in 1963 (age 27-28); no material design output milestone by age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Stuttgart as the grandson of Ferdinand Porsche and son of Ferry Porsche, F.A. Porsche attended the Ulm School of Design before being dismissed. He joined the family company in 1958, trained under design director Erwin Komenda, and took charge of the design department around 1962, leading to the creation of the Porsche 911 unveiled in 1963.
family_context_summary: Grandson of Porsche founder Ferdinand Porsche and son of Ferry Porsche; grew up on the family estate (Schüttgut) near the Porsche works in Zuffenhausen, spending hours in his grandfather's workshops as a child.
parent_family_domain_summary: Deep automotive design dynasty: grandfather Ferdinand Porsche designed the Volkswagen Beetle and founded the company; father Ferry Porsche led the company and directed the 911 project. F.A. was immersed in automotive engineering and design from birth.
evidence_summary: F.A. Porsche had extraordinary inherited advantages — grandson of the founder, son of the company leader, immersed in automotive design from childhood — but his landmark design, the Porsche 911, was not unveiled until the 1963 Frankfurt Motor Show when he was 27-28. While he took charge of the design department around 1961-62 (age 25-26), no material design output milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Anton LaVey
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: founded the Church of Satan in 1966 at age 36; before that he worked as a circus performer, organist, and crime scene photographer with no material independently verifiable milestone by age 26.
early_history_summary: Born Howard Stanton Levey in Chicago in 1930, LaVey grew up in the Bay Area and claimed to have joined the Clyde Beatty Circus at 16 as a cage boy and lion tamer. He later worked as an organist in burlesque shows and as a photographer, gradually cultivating occult interests before founding the Church of Satan in 1966.
family_context_summary: Born in Chicago to a family that moved to California soon after; parents were not documented in detail in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: LaVey's early biography is largely self-reported and difficult to verify. He claimed to have worked in a circus and as an organist, but no independently verifiable milestone occurred before age 26. His founding of the Church of Satan in 1966 at age 36 was his first material public achievement.

name: He Pingping
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: certified by Guinness World Records as the world's shortest mobile man in 2008 at age 19-20, but this was recognition of a congenital physical condition (primordial dwarfism), not a talent- or effort-based achievement milestone; died at age 21 in 2010.
early_history_summary: Born in Wulanchabu, Inner Mongolia, China in 1988 with primordial dwarfism, He Pingping appeared on Chinese television in January 2007 and was certified by Guinness World Records in 2008 as the world's shortest mobile man at 74.6 cm tall. He traveled internationally for media appearances before dying in Rome in 2010 at age 21.
family_context_summary: Born in Wulanchabu (Huade county), Inner Mongolia, China with primordial dwarfism; parents were villagers. No documented family advantages.
evidence_summary: He Pingping's Guinness World Record recognition at age 19-20 was based on a congenital physical condition (primordial dwarfism) rather than talent, effort, or skill development. While independently verifiable, this does not constitute a material achievement milestone in the sense intended by the rubric. He died at age 21 in 2010.

name: Zoltán Horváth
milestone_by_age_26: At age 20 in 1957, Horváth won World Championship team gold in sabre fencing at Paris; by age 26 he had won Olympic team gold and individual silver at the 1960 Rome Olympics and individual World Championship gold in 1962.
early_history_summary: Born in Balatonfüred, Hungary, Horváth began fencing at age 15 in Budapest for the Vasas club. He became a first-class fencer at 16, won a national youth championship at 17, and was selected for the Hungarian national team at 20. He joined Vörös Meteor in 1957 and became a key member of Hungary's dominant sabre fencing program through the 1960s.
family_context_summary: Born in Balatonfüred, Hungary; moved to Budapest at age 15 to fence. Father ran a stamp dealership, which Horváth later took over. No documented family fencing background.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as fencing-related; father was a stamp dealer.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Hungarian fencing, Vasas club, Vörös Meteor, national team, sabre tradition, Gerevich Kárpáti teammates
evidence_summary: Horváth's early advantage was immersion in Hungary's world-dominant sabre fencing ecosystem. He began fencing at 15 in Budapest, joined elite clubs (Vasas, then Vörös Meteor), and was fast-tracked into the national team by age 20. His teammates included Olympic legends like Aladár Gerevich and Rudolf Kárpáti, providing an exceptional peer environment. He won World Championship team gold at 20 and Olympic gold and silver at 23. No family fencing background or financial advantage was documented; his advantages were institutional and geographic.
starting_point: Born in 1937 in Balatonfüred, Hungary; moved to Budapest at age 15 to begin fencing at the Vasas club; father ran a stamp dealership.
current_position: Died June 12, 2025 at age 88 in Budapest; final role: retired fencer and former international fencing coach, later ran family stamp dealership.

trajectory.event: Won the Hungarian national youth championship in sabre fencing, establishing himself as a rising talent.
Won World Championship team gold in sabre at Paris, his first major international medal, after joining Vörös Meteor and the Hungarian national team.
Won Olympic team gold and individual silver in sabre at the Rome Olympics, finishing behind teammate Rudolf Kárpáti in the individual event.
Won individual World Championship gold in sabre at Buenos Aires, his greatest individual achievement.
Competed at the Tokyo Olympics, placing fifth in the team sabre event, before a car accident interrupted his career.
Won his final World Championship team gold in sabre at Moscow, capping his competitive career.
Died on June 12, 2025, in Budapest at age 88.
